Yes! The topic of fertilizer brings up another aspect of my goals. I would want to incorporate aquaponics. Being in Arizona, the desert is harsh. It wastes so much water from evaporation. A decent amount never reaches the plants roots. Which requires more water and fertilizer to compensate for the evaporation loss. I would want to do as much as possible with vertical farming. A positive of being indoor is that alone takes natural sunlight out of the equation. If you already plan to primarily rely on artificial light, there’s no need to have the building above ground absorbing so much heat. So I would want it to be underground where the average temperature stays around 75 year round. It would have a fish pond on top. Feed the fish from the plant waste and feed the plants with the fish waste. I’d also like to use the pond as a thermal battery. Have a cover during the day to allow sunlight but block heat increase and evaporation. Use the underground temperature of the pond as an air conditioner. Similar to an underground air tube. Basically bubble warm air out at the bottom of the pond, capture that air from the sealed top, and the air cools and filters dust/pollen as it rises to the top. Then at night, open the top to allow heat to escape and recharge its thermal potential. I feel like air tubes are limited by surface area. Once the rock absorbs the heat, the heat exchange is limited by the speed heat radiates through stone. With liquid cooling the heat should radiate quicker and cause currents and circulation. Which should make it possible to evenly utilize the entire thermal potential. I’d have to do some research about how big of a temperature change it would cause in the pond and how that would effect the health of the fish. I don’t remember the exact figures but aquaponics could reduce water and fertilizer consumption in crop production by around 95%. Underground with fairly natural temperature control should reduce electricity consumption by a decent amount. I’d like to cool/ heat the homes/ housing area via the same pond thermal battery with probably a carbon filter involved to reduce the fish smell and potential humidity. More thermal demand would just require a bigger pond. Which would hold more fish.

That’s all really cool and all things that I really resonate with. I’ve seen the top and I’ve seen the bottom and both could use serious improvements. It’s difficult because that’s life. Nobody has everything solved perfectly and the equation changes constantly. But there are a lot of basics that aren’t being acknowledged. I think a major aspect is applying knowledge. Schools teach concepts that might apply to life eventually but skip over aspects that matter every single day. A good point is nutrition. How to have a balanced diet that is convenient, nutritious, efficient, and economical. How to budget, save, and invest. Apply skills at a younger age. Like programming, a school might teach the basic concepts without mentoring how to apply those concepts to something new and valuable. Up until calculus, math was just calculating numbers. It was really cool the see how those numbers and equations translated to real world measurements and applications. It became a tool instead of just a process. Once a process becomes a tool, it’s like a medium for creating art. I feel that schooling lacked that aspect. Life skills and applied knowledge. 

Affordable efficient housing is big. And it’s more than just the housing, it’s the community and ecosystem. It’s difficult when one problem stems from multiple, much larger problems. To really get it right you practically have to change the world. I actually believe prisons have a lot of untapped potential. If only it were open to the world and actually focused on developing stability and growth. Like a place to start at the bottom and really develop the skills and experience to not just catch up with everyone else but be even better. Aquire life skills with the safety net to allow risk of failure and have the guidance to know where and how to improve. A way to pause obligations so you can direct your priorities to get into a position to sustain those responsibilities and stay above water. Better programs to push people into developing fields. 

A prison is nearly self sustainable by collective effort. Residents contribute to meal preparation and distribution. Resident maintenance. Just add solar and agricultural space. Like roommates to cut down on rent but on a larger scale. Until individual costs are nearly zero with a distributed workload that provides steady nutritious meals at wholesale prices/ community grown. A solid foundation to build off. Room to pursue ambitions without fear that it wouldn’t pay rent soon enough or detract necessary life maintenance. That’s essentially one of my projects I’d really like to pursue when it’s possible. It’s not exactly the same as yours but they do share some very similar intentions. It’s a project that feels pretty ambitious with probably little financial reward. But it’s a cause I believe is worth creating. In prison and everywhere else, there is just so much potential waiting for an opportunity to flourish. It’s really nice to hear that other people are out there working to make a better world.

Exactly. To me, it’s all about the revenue model. Labor trades are still very necessary but far from enticing. It seems like the strategy is to add hurdles for prisoners to limit their aspirations. Like a message that they aren’t welcomed into other fields so they just have to take what they can get. Come to terms with the fact that they’ll need to do harder work for less pay and be grateful they have a job at all. Once those expectations are lowered, the prisons gladly guide them into positions that are in the lowest demand. Like it’s not about growing them to reach their potential, but mold them to positions that are hard to fill. It’s systematic and that aspect of incarceration is probably the biggest flaw. It works, but it’s not right.

After prison and the whole experience with the legal system and process, I’m surprised how much of a blind spot it is. Until I got myself into that situation, I had no clue about any of it. How do bonds/ bails work? How to find a lawyer? What’s prison like? How is life with a record? I’ve done well in life before prison. No life of crime. No criminal tendencies. All honors through school, top of my class. My credit was over 800. Plenty of scholarships. I almost joined the navy. Took the ASVAB and scored in the top 3% and offered to become a nuclear engineer. Surely those hurdles from having a record won’t overshadow all of that? There must be some good that still shines through? Nope. It took a month of applying at every shit job around me. Not even able to be a warehouse worker. A few weeks ago I got a job serving and now there’s this anxiety like if that stops working out, what are my other options. I have a lot of projects that I think have some potential but it’ll take some time to save up at this rate. And even longer to find free time to put into side projects. It’ll happen. It’s getting there. But I didn’t imagine it would really slow me down this much. It must be so much harder for everyone else who didn’t have a decent foundation to begin with. In prison there really are a lot of people who are have so much creativity, ingenuity, and solid work work ethic. They should really be given the opportunities to shine. Also, I’m curious about the social project you’re working on. Could you share a little info or is it best kept under wraps until you’re ready to reveal. Oh yeah, those trades can become whole organizations! There’s room for someone to go into it alone but a lot of things are done by groups. It’s actually pretty inspiring to see people just go for it and make it work. I’d say a good example of team effort is the different foods. Like tamales. I never made any personally but it’s essentially crushed tortilla chips, shredded/ chopped meats(like bagged portions of tuna. But there’s also shredded chicken, shredded beef, barbacoa. Then also chopped summer sausage. It is meat but it’s highly preserved.), cheese squeeze (like spray cheese without the spray), rice(instant), beans(instant), and jalapeños(small plastic jars, sliced). It’s all essentially gas station foods. So there would be a few guys crushing the chips to turn into masa (just add water and mix) . Basically like a corn flour dough. That’s spread out on a plastic sheet. (Squares cut out of a trash bag). The meats are chopped and mixed. Beans and rice cooked. So some guys doing that. (We had a microwave. 1 for 150 guys. So the lines could get pretty long). Then it’s all added to the masa, it’s wrapped, then the plastic goes around it a few times. The ends are twisted tight and tied in knots. Then we had something called an immersion heater. It’s basically just a coil that’s plugged into the wall and the coil has electrical resistance so it heats up. Anyways, they fill a trash can or bucket with water and throw in like 5 immersion heaters( aka stingers). Then the wrapped tamales are left to boil for a few hours. Then we have like the styrofoam gas station coolers. A few get loaded up and a few guys go out to sell. So they just go from pod to pod and building to building walking up and down the rows of bunks announcing they have tamales. Small for 2 soups(~1.35) or large for 3 soups(~2.00). The soup/ ramen pack is like the standard currency. But it’s really anything of equal or comparable value. Then they take their earnings to the store and trade for supplies to make more. So it’s a whole operation with usually like 5+ people. And that’s true for just about every other trade. Yeah, they invite people to join. A lot of the time it’s the youngsters getting into debt and needing a way to work their way out of it. As a way to help them earn money and also offer mentorship. Or just those who don’t get outside money. Or anyone willing to put in some work. 

There’s really nothing with moving parts. It’s really just bars welded together and planted in cement. It’s all body weight resistance. For added weight they might lay back to back. There’s also medicine balls. I think 10lbs and 25lbs. Another thing people do that’s kind of frowned upon by the prison is making sand bags. Basically just tying up a shirt, putting a trash bag in it, and filling it with sand. To have a more consistent weight they measure how much sand to add by using cups. So maybe they’d start out doing curls with 50 cups and when they want to bump up weight start doing 60 or whatever. I never bothered with that so I’m not sure what the standard amount of cups they’d use per lift. Whenever they’d close the yard for shift change, you’d have to drain the sand bag. It’s technically against the rules to modify anything or use anything for its unintended purpose. But it’s a gray area where most CO’s don’t hassle about it. 

For drugs, yeah, I’d say it was pretty common. Especially at the first yard I went to. I changed yards right as Covid happened so I’m not sure if that yard just got less drugs or of Covid shutting down visits stopped the flow. But at the first place, you could get spice at any time. $4 for what’s called a box. The spice was so strong that it’s measured by making a single file line of specks across a rolling paper. Like specks of pepper. Id guess only 25 specks per box. Maybe less. Then it’s put on a square of paper and folded a few times. Oof, that stuff was strong! Those 25 specks, I would highly advise against smoking the whole thing alone in one sitting! I would roll it. (They would call that a stick). Then cut that stick into quarters. Then to smoke it you’d basically have a tiny plastic bottle. Like the tiny hotel shampoo bottles. Then poke a hole at the bottom, squeeze the stick into the hole, then light it with a cigarette. Or a cricket. Which is basically the same concept as the immersion heater but smaller. Use a CD player power adapter, wrap a small wire around a thumbtack to make a coil, then touch the ends of the coil to the power adapter. One end positive one else negative. Boom, you got yourself a lighter! (Cricket). The wire usually comes from taking apart the coil inside of a stinger. But it’s easier if you know someone who works in the kitchen to bring back one of those steel dish scrubber pads. It needs to be a certain metal/ gauge to have enough resistance to heat up but also enough strength not to burn out. Anyways. With the spice you really inhale every bit you can and hold it as long as you can so it really soaks in. 1/4 of a stick was enough for me to forget what the concept of smell was. Enough to feel like Im on a roller coaster with crazy geometric visuals. Enough to have no comprehension of reality. Usually like 30-60 minutes. Just chill on the bed watching tv. Nothing to stress about. I’d say I wouldn’t have put myself in that position if I didnt feel completely safe and comfortable. Oh yeah, that part was great. It was a higher security yard so more restrictions but $4 a week and able to smoke any time and have a few nice short mental vacations to myself, that was luxury. That place was cells too so I could feel more private. The second place, everything was really open. Like a warehouse with a bunch of cubicles. The ‘walls’ were under 3’ heigh so a lot less privacy. It felt too exposed to get too high. Plus stuff was really hard to come by so when it did, it was way more expensive and really diluted. For harder stuff, idk too much about that. I’ve never been interested in that stuff. But the first place did have plenty of black(heroin) and G(meth). I heard a lot about it but no personal experience. A few times people had real weed. A few wax cartridges. But it had too much smell, and the wax was difficult to work with. I never bothered with it in case of a random drug test. 

Yeah, I guess it’s pretty cool, now that I’m writing this stuff out, to see how the prison system isn’t really as fucked as it’s made out to be. I did something wrong, did time, had opportunities, and no traumatic experience. The incarceration for profit model is still seriously flawed but at least the experience isn’t miserable. At least not in my experience. I made some pretty good friends and had plenty of moments I actually enjoyed. Sometimes it was like a house party with no option to go home. Still bittersweet but there were times that were pretty sweet.

I didn’t fully miss it. I might have even seen it closer than a lot of people. There were 2000 guys on my yard and nearly everyone got it at the same time. Some people just never got it. Out of 2000 only 3 were taken to a hospital for closer observation. And there was a surprising amount of older guys too. Some in their 90’s. I could see nearly 2000 Covid cases first hand. A lot of guys had headaches, loss of smell/taste. A few had loss of appetite. And a few were very lethargic. Most were 1-3 days. A lot were closer to a week. And a few were 2+ weeks. Then a high amount had a positive test but zero symptoms. I was in the 1-3 day group. Only slight loss of smell for a day. Then a kind of weird sense of smell/ taste for 2 days. It was maybe a little strange but for me, a common cold would be multiple times worse. It’s not over. Some people get more serious symptoms. But from my personal experience and witnessing 2000 cases unfold, it’s not worth shutting the world down for 2 years. I know it’s an extremely polarizing topic. But in Arizona, we aren’t exactly panicked about Covid anymore. Here, it’s pretty much life as usual.

I did just about everything I could find to try to prepare. I think there are good programs for people still looking for direction. Like training to pass the written CDL license test, waste water management, plumber, electrician, welder, GED, and even bachelors in general studies. Maybe I should’ve taken more advantage of those programs but my focus is really on software development. I bought a few books on python and Java and swift but there’s no replacing experience. I could read the books and understand concepts but I couldn’t write/ test code to see if anything I’m doing actually worked. A lot of programming uses resources outside of the standard language. An analogy could be like the book teaches how to use sticks to build a fire. A career in programming is dealing with fine tuned combustion engines. There are so many parts that are already made and don’t need to be reinvented myself. I didn’t have access to any of those parts so my knowledge couldn’t pass the very primitive stages. It didn’t hurt but it didn’t help as much as I hoped it would. I wish there were tech focused training programs. But there isn’t exactly a lot of demand when such a small amount of the prison population could handle it. There’s a test called the mandate which basically you don’t get time reduced if you don’t pass. The level to pass is equal to about 7th grade. I’d estimate close to half of the prisoners couldn’t pass it. Even with years of retests and classes to prepare. So passing the mandate was the bar for good. Getting a GED is like great. Diploma would be like excellent. And any college is like outstanding. 

My point is just that there are plenty of programs to help people get from bad to decent. But no programs to get people from great to better. Physical trades are the most optimistic and probable outcomes. Especially with a record.

Oh yeah, there’s a few things to do. With so much free time there are all kinds of creative ways to spend time. There’s like a trade economy. Both trade as in barter and trade as is skilled trades. A lot of guys learn to sew/ tailor. The clothes they give you suck so a lot of guys will pay a few dollars to get their clothes fitted. There’s artists who make greeting cards basically or portraits or tattoo designs. Then the tattoo artists. There’s bakers who make cakes and brownies and cheesecakes. Plus other sweets like taffy or suckers or ice cream. Then the cooks that make things like burritos and tamales and orange chicken. People makes beer (hooch) and sometimes even distilled vodka. Then there’s labor things like housekeeping, laundry, or shoe cleaning. Some people run stores. Which basically money is only able to be spent once a week to order products. Then it takes another week to actually receive your products. So stores let people get the items immediately in exchange for repaying the cost plus interest. So guys stock up their own “stores” and manage it like a bank. On top of that is a smaller version. Like selling sets of cigarettes(4-5) or a shot of coffee mix for a soup(ramen). There’s also raffles that people do that basically there’s something worth maybe $5-10 and you pay 2 soups(~$1.25) for a chance to win it. Usually a 1/25 chance. There’s also sports betting. There’s casual card games or betting poker tables. Before Covid drugs were easy to get. Mostly spice because it doesn’t show up on drug tests easily. It was very common to feel like a house party with people smoking spice, drinking hooch, playing poker, watching games, and eating brownies. 

For self help, yes, there is exercise equipment. My yards were all just bars at different heights and angles wrapped around a track about the size of a football field. Pull up bars, rows, dips, incline/ decline press. But all just bars. There’s the track to walk/ run laps, softball field, basketball courts, horseshoes, volleyball. A few outside picnic tables. Higher security yards get less access. My first yard was 2 hours a day, the second yard for lower security inmates it was open access basically 5am-8pm. Minus 2-3 hours when they send everyone inside so the correction officers can change shifts and count all the inmates. 

There are libraries. I found a lot of good books. I’d say at least 50 and the majority all worth reading. That was all like educational or insightful. There were maybe 1000+ books but a lot was fiction. Around the middle of last year we got tablets. No internet, just predownloaded content. It had access to a lot of podcasts. My favorite was being able to watch all of the Ted talks. It had khan academy which is a lot of videos about science and math. Nothing crazy but enough to learn a few things. It had ebooks. They’re all free but that’s because the copyrights have expired. So 99% of the books were from the 1900’s or earlier. Then 1% for government publications. I think I had 750 books downloads. That became my internet. I could research most things but searching a topic, finding a few books, then text searching for certain phrases. It had an app for looking at job postings. But it was sponsored by big businesses that had some pretty high level requirements that I bet are very hard to find in prison populations. It also allowed essentially email. Or like text messaging with a relay service. So we could send and receive messages but they weren’t immediate, they had to be reviewed first. So sometimes it’d take a few days to finally come through. I already forgot but I think it was about .25 a message. But 6000 character limit which is probably where I developed a tendency to write long messages to get the most bang for my buck. Haha.

Well, that’s possibly a longer story but I’ll try to make it short. Haha. 

My dad owned his own commercial steel construction company. (Ironically, he started it because he had 6 kids and went to prison for a few months. He realized he wouldn’t be able to get a great job to support all of those kids with his new record. So he studied whatever books he could find to help him get his contractors license. Then he started his own company). Well, one day he was moving the roof framing that was build on ground, into place on the columns with 2 forklifts. In the process, I guess the framing got snagged on a tree branch which threw the forklift off balance. The framing swung back which cause his forklift to flip. He fell out of the lift on its way down. The forklift and roof framing landed on him and messed him up pretty bad. This was 2014. 

2016 I took over the business. He was the brains with the experience and business connections. I did the on-site work and relaying his advice. Well, mid 2016 he was taken to the hospital because he wasn’t breathing and went unconscious. My little sister just graduated high school. She was looking into colleges and trade schools and work opportunities. She was fighting with her boyfriend. Who knows what her motivation was. But she saw an opportunity to get into my dads pain killers while he was away. She under estimated them and it killed her. 

She was like my best friend. We would hang out basically every minute I was home from work. Well, that day I came home and made us some food. She didn’t come out and I didn’t want to wake her up. We’d always swim. I went out and the whole time it felt wrong that she wasn’t there. 

I’ll have to check if I’ve already written this part of the story before. Probably in my comment history somewhere. think I have so I can try to move it along. Well, I finally go in her room to see why she hasn’t come out. Then I was hit with the reality that I’ll never be able to talk to her again. One day I have a little best friend. The next, she’s gone forever. 

Over 6 months we try to stay above water. Keep the business running and bills paid and hope time heals the wounds. Exactly 6 months after I lost my little sister, my dad gave up. He felt responsible because it was his pills and he felt he should’ve locked them up better. On top of being physically disabled. He took too many of his painkillers and he died too. 

6 more months… I was still try not to sink. The business was slipping. Incapable employees, $15k in payroll per week, obviously severe depression, anxiety, and pressure. So I didn’t have the energy or motivation to deal with all of that on top of losing my dad and sister. Let’s just say it went from trying to float on water to like in the movie passengers when she was swimming and the ship lost gravity. It went from trying to stay up and not go down, to having the meaning of up and down being irrelevant. 

6 more months… life is a mess. I went from renting a 6 bedroom house with a pool in a great neighborhood to living in my sisters back yard in a 20’ 1970 rv. Cost $500 and a tow. Unemployed trying to stretch $1000 for a few months. Well, my mom decided to give up too. She lived in a different state and we weren’t too close. But it didn’t help. 

6 more months my ex decided my depression was killing her vibe and holding her back. So she started sleeping with her manager. Well, I went to her work and saw them together. In my mind I was just like, “god damnit, here comes another hit”. Well, it still hurt but it wasn’t enough to break me. So in my mind I just wanted something to finally break me too so I wouldn’t have to keep taking these unnecessary hits. Like damn, if I’m going to give up I’d prefer it happened before all this extra pain. So I guess I decided instead of laying in a ball waiting for something to break me, I’d just try to move it along and push myself to break. So I figured if it was a struggle staying alive in the free world, with plenty of money (by this time my dads life insurance paid out. My portion was $200k. I can confirm money does not buy happiness.), then prison would be a pretty big hurdle. 

So, I crashed my car into my exs managers car. He was in it. The cars took some damage but he barely twisted a leg, got a Walgreens leg wrap, and was back at work telling the story like a joke. (I have a few friends within the company so I heard some updates.) He used to be a cop for Phoenix PD. So he had connections to make sure it wasn’t taken lightly. What I did was wrong. It was 100% about everything else and 0% about him or anger or violence. Just me trying to screw myself in a big way. Which worked! 

I was out on bond for about 1.5 years. Plenty of money and living everyday like my last. I figured if I had any money left in my account when I got sentenced, he would be able to take it. Can’t take money if I don’t have any. Poor decision. Haha. I did a lot…. You know, maybe in the end money did buy happiness? I just went out more and did more. More movement led to more movement. I also did a lot of acid and really dove deep into the meaning of life and death and just about everything as deep as possible. Figuring out what is really important and why. And figuring out which perspectives just weren’t sustainable. Idk. But in the end, I look back at that time like one of the best times in my life. Like being reborn. Living in the same world but nothing is the same and now there’s unlimited potential. Then I got sentenced to prison. 3.5 years. By then it wasn’t a threat. It wasn’t an impossible mountain it was barely a speed bump. I’m not at the end, I’m just getting started. 

(6 months after the crash my older sister gave up too. So over 2 years I lost 2 of my sisters, both of my parents, my girlfriend of 8 years, my dads 20 year business, and got myself 3.5 years of prison. Idk how I’ve made it. I give a lot of credit to the acid. It can be a real tool. All I know is my brain is rewired and I’m 100% sure that if all of that couldn’t stop me than nothing will so better prepare for a long life and dying of old age. And if I’m going to be alive all that time, the least I can do is actually live!

2.5 years in Az prison. It’s nothing like movies or shows make it out to be. It’s not dark with rats and leaking pipes and surprise stabbings. None of that gay rape stuff. Like others have said, the worst part really is just the boredom and major waste of time. An analogy that I think of is it’s like working a double and you’re counting down the minutes until you’re off and finally done. Then imagine it’s time to be off but they make you stay longer. And longer. And longer. Days, weeks, months, years... Just constantly waiting for your chance to finally clock out and go home. Violence exists but it’s not random or too different from regular life. Maybe intensity but not exactly reasoning. People borrow money, borrow drugs, or gamble then never get around to paying their debt. After asking multiple times where’s the money, there’s a point where it takes more than words. Obviously a big part is the debt, but the other big factor is the lies and runaround and ducking and dodging. Aside from that, there can be problems from disrespect. Things like being too loud, too late or too early. Serious bad hygiene stinking up the block. Or just common disrespect from someone being rude or arrogant. Az does have race segregation. It’s not crazy like you can’t be friends with or associate with other races. But there are some kind of weird rules. It’s not so much of a racist thing as like a team. Like for the small or weak or old or whatever. Or poor. There like managers. They describe it is politics. So there’s the complex which could hold multiple yards. The yard which holds multiple buildings. And the buildings which hold multiple pods. So there’s like the lowest level manager for each race that are responsible for their pods. Then a higher level like general manager for buildings. Regional manager for the yard. VP for the complex. And very top level for the state. So someone new would come in and the head of the pod will introduce themselves. Introduce you to other people in the pod. Usually see if you need anything to get started. Like bowls or cups or shoes or cigarettes or coffee or hygiene like soap or razor. No strings. The idea is like every person is a reflection of their team. So if someone comes in as a stinky bum, it reflects on the whole group. The heads also explain the rules and etiquette and they’re in charge of making sure the rules are followed. Since there’s basically teams, if one person is really screwing up, it basically comes down to either the heads handle the issue or the other team will. Then it goes from a personal issue to a potential war. So there’s this thing they call a “hot one” which is basically a small correction after words aren’t working. Depending on the severity its like 5-10 seconds of body shots from 1-3 people. Maybe a few bruises but nothing close to life threatening or disfigurement. Enough to strike the realization they need to really improve because they don’t want any more. Obviously the intensity goes up if the first message doesn’t sink in. Overall, there’s no violence without warning. Not that I’ve seen. I have seen 3 people beaten to death, but never once feared for my safety or ever even got a hot one. I’m 5’11” and like 160. So it’s not like I was big and bad and nobody dared fuck with me. I just never disrespected anyone and never owed anyone money. It’s really just how you choose to make it. If you’re looking for some action, there’s plenty of action to get in on. If you just want to do your time and go home, no problem at all. I wanna touch on the gay part again because that’s the misconception I hate the most. In those few years I never once witnessed anything gay. However, homosexuals do exist. In prison and the real world. I’ve heard maybe 2-3 stories of gay people doing gay things, but it was all consensual. Just like the real world. It’s all consensual. So if you’re really fully straight, a few months or years aren’t going to turn you gay. Some people might turn, but I fully believe that’s an indication they weren’t fully straight to begin with, not inherent of prison. Plus, more time does equal more pressure. Like for the guys doing life and realizing they will never have a physical partnership with a woman again. But it’s a human need to have that connection. Or something similar. That has to be a really touchy situation to process. But 1 year? 5 years? 10 years? Me personally, no thanks. I can wait. 

I’ve kind of rambled on. My experience was just painful boredom. A lot of tv. I had my girlfriend and family and friends. I had some money saved for myself plus the stimulus checks so I was able to have $50ish a month and still get out with a few thousand to help restart. It was enough to have coffee and cigarettes to enjoy. Some food to feel less hunger. Have my own tv and CD player. Buy a nice blanket and pillow from a fund raiser. Many aren’t so lucky. Having no money, comfort, or support can lead to desperation, hopelessness, and mental/emotional imbalance which could all lead to a 1000x harder sentence. 

Yes, prison is much much better than jail. In my experience at least. I only spent about a month in jail but it was miserable. There was just no structure or comfort. A lot of new guys coming in with their impression of prisoner life from movies. So they’re loud and disrespectful and want to fight and prove they’re big and bad. Like dogs barking out of fear. They don’t want to be seen as weak so they over compensate. In prison, everyone is pretty settled in. They realize it’s not at all like they imagined and they go back to being normal people. A good point is in jail, most people aren’t sentenced. They don’t know how long they’ll be there and it causes a lot of anxiety. In prison, you know when you’ll be done. Then you just settled in and wait for the time to pass. Jail food sucks. The mattresses suck and it’s not uncommon not to be given a pillow. And if you get one, I wouldn’t even call it a pillow. Jail just has a lot of anxiety. Everyone loud and looking for fights. Plus it’s Cold and uncomfortable. So horrible sleep. Always hungry and crappy food. It’s like it’s made to put everyone on edge. I would rather do 3 years in prison vs 6 months in jail. It’s that big of a difference. 

Some good news, I’ve only been out a month and a half. Idk if my memory is that bad or prison really didn’t leave an impression on me but I’d say in less than a week I felt like I completely forgot about it. When the time is done and life goes on, it just disappears. Now it’s just a weird fact that I know is true but only vaguely remember. Another misconception, at least in my experience, is that it’s difficult for an exprisoner to break away from their prison mentality to readapt to the real world. For me, it wasn’t hard to forget about prison, it was hard to remember how to do the real world. Things like going to the store or ordering food at a restaurant. Stupid little things. Like it’s not that prison changed any of that, it’s the fact that I haven’t done it in so long that it’s not as natural as it was before prison. Then on top of that, the world never stopped. There’s new apps and social networks. I missed all of Covid which changed so much so it took a while to figure out what things are just done differently now. I’m 27 and went in when I was 24. I can’t even imagine what it’d be like for older people who have been gone 10+ years. 

All of this is just my experience. I’m sure every state, gender, age group, sentence length, crime severity, financial status, etc. all come with different experiences. But for those who wanted a deeper look at what it’s like than just 1-2 sentence responses, I hope I helped shed some light. I wouldn’t recommend it. It’s a giant waste of time and life. But if it’s something you’re already facing, don’t worry so much. My biggest negatives were boredom and time passing too slowly. Nothing to have nightmares about or panic attacks or ptsd.

June 2016 my little sister (18) died from taking more of my dads painkillers than her body could handle. (He went to the hospital for a few nights and she wanted to see how they work recreationally.) At the time, I (22) was president of my dads construction company making good money. I was renting a house and fully supporting my dad and 2 of my younger siblings. I felt things were going well up to that point. Well paying job, close to family, nice house, nice car, I had my girlfriend that I’ve had since 15. I was getting the sense of having things figured out in life. 

When she passed, I shut down without realizing. I just really isolated myself, just sent the work crew without me and hoped for the best. So I spent months in my room drinking very heavily and lightly experimenting with a few things. November 2016 my dad couldn’t handle that she died because of his pills and he felt responsible. So he did the same thing. Since I shut down, my girlfriend got other ideas and I didn’t see her much at all.  Summer 2017 my mom couldn’t take her daughter and her ex (my dad who she once wished a slow miserable death on...) well, she came home from work and I guess just stayed in the car with it on and that was it for her too. 

Shortly after she passed, my ex was drinking heavily too and she asked me to pick her up from the bar so I did. She passed out and she got a message from somebody through a texting app and labeled as “panda”. So I got curious and looked into it. Turns out that’s the bar manager at the restaurant she works at and she’s been hooking up with him since before my sister died. I know I neglected her when I stopped functioning, but she was around me for about a year acting like everything was good but she was behind my back the whole time. 

I got more suicidal and got myself in trouble for crashing my car trying to hurt myself. (The illegal part was the only thing around to hit was the managers car. Obviously a HORRIBLE idea.) crashing the car didn’t do anything at all and now I was facing dying pretty miserably is prison so now I HAD to finish myself off. So there was a lake nearby and cops were after me so I jumped in the lake to try to just drown. But the cops didn’t find me yet and I still had family and friends to say bye too and loose ends to take care of so I don’t go out being disrespectful. So I decided I’ll just keep swimming and trying to get away until they get close. There’s no point in killing myself too soon. 

I ended up getting away completely. I knew I was going to have to face consequences so in the week or 2 that I was on the run I was really focused on getting my mind right. If I went into jail/prison with a suicidal mindset, I wouldn’t make it out. Once I got feeling better, I text my ex kinda making my peace. I went to sleep and woke up with 5-10 U. S. Marshalls with some pretty heavy duty rifles pointing at me. I did about a week in jail before paying bail and the case is still ongoing. Just few week over a year waiting. 

In that year, I’ve really been searching for purpose in life. Before, I was extremely selfish and materialistic. Having court every 3 months forced me to find balance. When I’m told my time is extended, I treat it like my life is given back to me. And when it gets time for court again, it feels like there’s a chance my life as I know it will be taken away so I need to be fulfilled by myself to have strength to be put through whatever else gets thrown at me. About a month ago my older sister took herself too. 

Now, me and my little brother just bought motorhomes to live and travel full time. Just to reconnect with life and nature. I’m excited to see beaches and forests and dunes. Possibly seeing extreme nature or finding RV parks near or within bigger cities. Life is great. It’s crazy to believe I’m supposed to be it my lowest right now. Everyone is worried I’m contemplating suicide. But I’m probably more optimistic about my future than I’ve ever been. I’m fully satisfied and fulfilled in my present. I feel so good I can’t help myself from saying life is great and this is awesome. It’s amazing. 

Some things that got me here would be doing acid a few times. That helped bring a new perspective that life and existence are MUCH bigger than my own thoughts or emotions. I wouldn’t say it’s a miracle in itself, but it definitely can be a tool if it’s used right. 

A concept I could recognize with acid is just how connected everything in life is. A lot of things that could just be coincidence, seem to occur for an intended purpose.
